note: First verification pass on Chicago, web research from zero (no register). Delivered 3 verified candidates to data/research/chicago-verified.json (chi_001 to chi_003), below the 4-tree floor for a page. leads = trees that failed only on our evidence bar or on the count, raw material for a future pass. blocked = trees that must never ship whatever happens later, each with its reason. 2026-08-09 pass: found the Illinois Big Tree Register feature-service endpoint and delivered chi_004 (Champion Boxelder, Edgebrook Golf Course) to data/research/chicago-verified.json, bringing Chicago to 4 verified trees, the floor for a page.

leads.name: University of Chicago Main Quadrangle bur oak / black oak stand
leads.species: Bur Oak (Quercus macrocarpa) and Black Oak (Quercus velutina), mixed stand
leads.location_hint: Humanities Quadrangle and Social Sciences Quadrangle, University of Chicago main campus, Hyde Park, roughly 41.789, -87.5997
leads.why_not_shipped: Two native oak stands predate the University (founded 1890) and were deliberately preserved by trustee Judge Daniel Shorey when the quadrangles were laid out; a Chicago Maroon student column (2019) and a University of Chicago Magazine piece both confirm old oaks still stand in the quads today, and a University Facilities article (paywalled behind the intranet.uchicago.edu React app, could not be fetched by curl or WebFetch in this pass, both redirected to a JS-only shell) reportedly discusses the stand's history in more depth per search-engine summaries only, which is not something to trust without reading the source directly. No confirmed age figure or exact single-tree location was found that would clear the two-source bar for a specific collectible point; the sources describe a stand/cluster across two quads, not one tree with one place to stand. Worth a dedicated pass: visit or find the facilities.uchicago.edu article through a cached/archived copy, or contact UChicago Facilities (contact was named in secondary coverage: Richard Bumstead, associate director of campus environment) to pin an exact specimen and age.
leads.update_2026_08_08: The intranet source was read in a browser session: it quotes Goodspeed's History of the University of Chicago. Key passage: 'Judge Shorey was also the principle advocate for preserving the existing oaks on campus - oaks that in many cases predate the University.' Also: in the University's first year the western side was 'flat, but dry and covered with young oaks', so the preserved oaks were YOUNG in 1892, putting them at roughly 140-170 years now, not ancient. History is now double-sourced; what still fails is the collectible-point rule: every source describes a stand across two quadrangles, no single tree with one place to stand. Only a source naming one individual tree reopens this.

leads.name: Graceland Cemetery arboretum (unspecified individual specimen)
leads.species: unknown - cemetery is a certified Morton Arboretum-affiliate arboretum of 2,000+ trees, 103+ species, including American Elm
leads.location_hint: Graceland Cemetery, 4001 N Clark St, Uptown, Chicago, roughly 41.9556, -87.6598
leads.why_not_shipped: Graceland publishes its own self-guided Tree Tour maps (PDF, e.g. https://www.gracelandcemetery.org/images/Tree_Tour_II_Map_-_to_be_added_to_website.pdf) which likely name specific notable specimens, but the tour pages fetched in this pass described the collection only in aggregate, with no individual tree's age, species or exact plot called out. A future pass should open the actual Tree Tour PDF map(s) rather than the landing page; if they name specific champion or notably old trees with locations, that could produce one or more strong candidates within a 25 to 30 minute transit ride of downtown (Red Line to Sheridan or Berwyn, or Clark St bus).
leads.update_2026_08_08: Both PDF tour maps (Tree Tour I, 50 numbered specimens, and Tree Tour II, 50 more) were opened and read in full this pass. Both are plain species-identification walks, one example of each species numbered on a map (White Pine, Bur Oak is not even listed; the closest natives are a Northern Pin Oak, a Pin Oak, an English Oak, a Black Oak and a Swamp White Oak scattered among ornamentals like Ginkgo, Katsura and Star Magnolia). Neither map gives an age, a girth, a 'champion' or 'notable' designation, or any text distinguishing one specimen as remarkable versus another; they exist to show garden diversity, not veteran trees. Targeted searches for a named old/champion tree at Graceland (elm survivor, champion oak, historic specimen) returned nothing beyond the same aggregate 'certified arboretum, 2,000+ trees' framing. This lead is now closed unless a future pass finds a specific news piece or arborist report naming one Graceland tree with an age and a plot location; the tour maps themselves are exhausted.

leads.name: University of Chicago Laboratory Schools courtyard oak
leads.location_hint: UChicago Laboratory Schools, Blaine courtyard/playground, 1362 E 59th St, Hyde Park, roughly 41.789, -87.596
leads.why_not_shipped: 2026-08-09 pass: same DNAinfo 2016 article that sourced chi_001 mentions 'a similarly sized oak tree in the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools courtyard', quoting the school's communications director and an alumna saying 'no one there could estimate its age'. No age, no second source beyond this one article, and the tree now sits inside a school playground/courtyard project (Culliton Quinn 'UChicago Lab Schools Playground | Blaine Courtyard', a climbable tree house built around a large oak at the courtyard's north entry corner) which raises a real access question: a K-12 school courtyard is not obviously open to the public the way a park or cemetery is. Would need: an age estimate from any source, confirmation the courtyard is publicly accessible (or specifically excluded if not), and ideally a look at whether the tree house construction has harmed the tree.

leads.name: Old growth oak / "Council" tree, Beverly / Blue Island Ridge
leads.location_hint: Somewhere on the Blue Island glacial ridge, Beverly neighbourhood (Ridge Historic District) or the separate suburb of Blue Island immediately south; exact location not found
leads.why_not_shipped: 2026-08-09 pass: a Beverly Review 'Good News 2022' piece quotes Robert Lane of the Ridge Historical Society describing an old-growth oak on the Blue Island ridge plausibly used by Native Americans travelling the Vincennes Trail, connected to events 'spanning 700 years'. The source article itself returned HTTP 429 on WebFetch (retry after a delay did not clear it in this pass) so the claim is second-hand via search snippet only, with no address, coordinates, current photo, or age figure. A 'Council Oak Montessori School' exists in Blue Island (the separate south-suburban town, not the Chicago neighbourhood of Beverly), suggesting local naming lore but not a specific standing tree. Needs: the actual Beverly Review article read in full (retry the fetch), or a direct approach to the Ridge Historical Society (ridgehistory@hotmail.com, cited in other coverage) to name and locate the specific tree, plus a check on whether Blue Island proper is within the ~30 minute day-trip boundary (it has a Metra Rock Island District stop, roughly 30 min from LaSalle Street Station, so it is borderline).

leads.name: The Sago Palm (cycad) of Lincoln Park Conservatory's Fern Room
leads.species: possibly Cycas circinalis or Cycas revoluta (sources vary), a cycad, not a true tree
leads.location_hint: Lincoln Park Conservatory, Fern Room, 2391 N Stockton Dr, Lincoln Park, Chicago
leads.why_not_shipped: 2026-08-09 pass: multiple travel-blog style sources (flowerchick.com and pages that appear to echo it) describe a 'century-old' sago palm/cycad in the Fern Room, said to have been an attraction people traveled to see during the 1893 World's Fair. The Conservatory's OWN official page (lincolnparkconservancy.org) only describes cycads generically ('among the most ancient group of plants... fossil records dating back at least 250 million years') with no mention of this specific dated specimen, so the striking claim has exactly one real source, repeated rather than corroborated. Two more open questions before this could ship even with a second source: exact species (sources conflict on the Latin name) and whether a potted greenhouse specimen fits the collectible-point / 'walk to a tree outdoors' product at all, which is a judgement call for a session with Hidde rather than a verification pass. Worth a future pass: ask the Chicago Park District or Lincoln Park Conservancy directly, or find a Chicago Tribune / local news piece with a acquisition date.

blocked.name: Bur Oak, Lincoln Park Zoo South Lawn
blocked.location_hint: Lincoln Park Zoo, South Lawn, Chicago
blocked.reason: DEAD. This was Chicago's best-known candidate for oldest tree (estimated 250-300 years, predating the city and the USA), but it was removed by crane and chainsaw crews on 2023-05-02 after reaching the end of its life cycle; confirmed by Block Club Chicago, WTTW, NPR and Smithsonian Magazine, all archived. 36 scions were grafted at the Morton Arboretum to preserve its genetics, but the tree itself is gone. Never ship as a living entry.

blocked.name: Birdhouse Oak, Lincoln Park (near Farm in the Zoo)
blocked.location_hint: 1911 N Stockton Dr, Lincoln Park, Chicago, across from the Farm in the Zoo
blocked.reason: Source (Block Club Chicago, 2022) describes it explicitly as a 'dying oak tree' that was given a second life as a public-art bird sanctuary with 190 birdhouses attached, i.e. a snag/dying specimen rather than a living, thriving tree. Fails the 'alive now' bar as reported; would need a fresh 2025/2026 check to see whether it is still standing and whether calling it 'alive' would be honest, or whether it is functionally a dead-tree art installation (which the project's dead-tree rule excludes as a collectible entry regardless of fame).

blocked.name: Massacre Tree (Fort Dearborn cottonwood)
blocked.location_hint: 18th Street between Prairie Avenue and the lake, Chicago
blocked.reason: DEAD since 1894. A cottonwood said to have been a sapling during the 1812 Fort Dearborn Massacre; a Chicago Tribune report of 1894-05-18 recorded it fell in a storm, was sawn in two and given to G. Pullman for his gardens. Historical-only, never a living entry.

blocked.name: "Champion" white oak, Pioneer Woods
blocked.location_hint: Pioneer Woods, Willow Springs, Cook County (Forest Preserve District of Cook County)
blocked.reason: Roughly 300 years old per the Forest Preserves' resource-management director, but Willow Springs is a distant southwest suburb, well outside the ~30 minute day-trip boundary of downtown Chicago. Same exclusion applies to the Millennium Landmark Tree at Morton Arboretum in Lisle (330+ years, white oak) — genuinely one of the region's oldest trees but a different city's day trip, not Chicago's.

blocked.name: Heritage Bur Oak, 244 N Forest Ave, Oak Park
blocked.location_hint: 244 N Forest Ave, Oak Park, IL
blocked.reason: DEAD. Roughly 200 years old, part of the same Oak Park heritage-oak cohort as the Kenilworth Witness Oak (chi_006) but a different, specific tree. Confirmed removed 2025-10-06 after developing disease following storm damage to a major limb; oakpark.com, 'After 200 years, beloved tree sees its last autumn' (2025-10-01). Never ship as a living entry.
